new_statements.quote: In Tangkhul languages, stress is always predictable. Only roots bear stress, and prefixes never bear stress. The preferred stress pattern, for a word (and foot), is iambic or anapestic. That is to say, a stem usually consists of a stressed (heavy syllable) root and one or two unstressed (light syllable) prefixes. Suffixes that are not a stem in their own right are not stressed, but these often form part of the same stressed syllable as the root.
new_statements.citation: Mortensen, David. 2003. Comparative Tangkhul. Unpublished ms. (qualifying paper), University of California, Berkeley, 17 December 2003. 73 pp.
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File (73 pp., dvipdfm, CreationDate 17 Dec 2003; title page 'Comparative Tangkhul, David Mortensen, University of California, Berkeley, December 17, 2003'). extracted text of PDF pp. 11-12 gives sec. 3.1 'Prefixes and Stress' word for word as quoted; the quote runs across the p.11/p.12 break ('...one or two unstressed (light syllable) | prefixes. Suffixes that are not a stem...'). Surrounding section: sec. 3 (p. 11) lists as a synchronic reason for grouping lexical and productive prefixes together '1. They do not bear stress, unlike root syllables'; p. 9 transcription note says the symbol for stressed /@/ allophone occurs 'in roots' while @ marks 'prefixal syllables'; sec. 3.2 (p. 12) adds…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is fully predictable from morphology: it falls on the root syllable; the one or two prefix syllables preceding it are unstressed light (sesquisyllabic) syllables and suffixes do not take stress, so in a prefixed word the stressed syllable is the final heavy root syllable (iambic/anapestic foot).
new_statements.exceptions: None stated for stress. Author notes prefix tone may be contrastive in some numerals and nouns (sec. 3.2), and that Huishu tone judgments are 'tentative at best' (p. 8).
new_statements.domain_note: Word/stem level: stress belongs to the root syllable; prefixes (lexical and grammatical, one or two) are unstressed light syllables, non-stem suffixes are unstressed and often fuse into the root syllable; foot described as iambic or anapestic. Statement is made for 'Tangkhul languages' as a group (Standard Tangkhul/Ukhrul, Kachai, Huishu); Huishu data are the author's own elicitation but thinner than Kachai (p. 8).
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog nort3286 'Northern Tangkhul Naga' = the speech of Huishu village (NE Ukhrul District, Manipur), no ISO code; Wikipedia 'Huishu language'. The quoted statement is made for the Tangkhul (Tangkhulic) group as a whole, based on the author's field data on Standard Tangkhul/Ukhrul (nmf, tang1336), Kachai (Glottolog East Tusom (east2902) and Sorbung are separate languoids.

sources.note: Sec. 3.1 'Prefixes and Stress' (pp. 11-12): in Tangkhul languages stress is always predictable; only roots bear stress, prefixes never; preferred word/foot pattern iambic or anapestic (one or two unstressed light prefix syllables + stressed heavy root); non-stem suffixes unstressed. Group-level statement covering Standard Tangkhul, Kachai and Huishu (Huishu data from the author's own elicitation, p. 8; Huishu tone judgments called tentative).
